There are 2 mailboxes in the MCI. Each Mailbox component of the MCI allows for secure and restricted communication between external SoC entities and the MCU. This communication channel is essential for exchanging control messages, status updates, and other critical information that the MCU will use to monitor system boot, firmware updates, and security critical operations. Section: Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Limited Trusted AXI users
Section text (lines 1296-1302):


There are 5 trusted AXI Users determined at build time via parameters or via MCI lockable registers. These users, a default user 0xFFFF_FFFF, and MCU are the only AXI users that can access or obtain a lock on the mailbox.

Any untrusted AXI user trying to read or write the mailbox will receive an AXI error response ([MCU Mailbox Errors](#mcu-mailbox-errors)).

Trusted users always have read access to the CSRs in the mailbox, but require MBOX [lock](#mcu-mailbox-locking) to write the CSRs. SRAM reads and writes require the trusted user to be the current [exclusive SRAM owner](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership).

Document: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md
Section: Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Locking
Section text (lines 1304-1313):


A Requester will read the "LOCK" register to obtain a lock on the mailbox. This is a read-set register, the lock is acquired when read returns 0. The Requester must be a [Trusted user](#mcu-mailbox-limited-trusted-axi-users). Once the lock is obtained the Requester has read access to the mailbox CSRs and, while the Requester is the current [SRAM owner](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership), write access to:

- CMD, DLEN and EXECUTE registers
- mailbox SRAM

Unlocking/releasing occurs when the current SRAM owner writes 0 to the EXECUTE register. The Requester can release only while it owns the SRAM: before it writes `EXECUTE=1`, or after ownership returns to it. Once `EXECUTE=1` hands the SRAM to Root, the Requester cannot abort the transaction. After releasing the mailbox the SRAM is zeroed out([MCU Mailbox SRAM Clearing](#mcu-mailbox-sram-clearing)).

On MCI reset release the MCU MBOX is locked for MCU. The MCU shall set the DLEN to the size of the SRAM and release the MBOX, causing the SRAM to be zeroed. This is done to prevent data leaking between warm resets via the SRAM.

Section: Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Status Registers
Section text (lines 1418-1447):


`CMD_STATUS` and `TARGET_STATUS` use the following encodings:

| Value | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 0 | BUSY |
| 1 | DATA_READY |
| 2 | COMPLETE |
| 3 | FAILURE |

The two status registers serve different polling domains. Only MCU writes
`CMD_STATUS`, and the original Requester polls it. Only the current Target
writes `TARGET_STATUS`, and MCU reads it. A terminal Target status shall not be
visible as command completion to the original Requester until MCU separately
writes a terminal `CMD_STATUS`.

Hardware resets `TARGET_STATUS` to BUSY on each Target handoff.

`CMD_STATUS` is not used when MCU is the Requester, because there is no
external Requester to serve. In that case MCU reads `TARGET_STATUS` directly.

`MBOX_HW_STATUS.SRAM_OWNER` reports the current exclusive SRAM owner:

| Value | Owner |
|---:|---|
| 0 | None |
| 1 | Requester/lock holder |
| 2 | Root AXI user, typically MCU |
| 3 | Target selected by `TARGET_USER` while `TARGET_USER_VALID=1` |

Section: Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox SRAM Clearing
Section text (lines 1461-1474):


When the mailbox lock is released the SRAM is zeroed out from 0 to max DLEN set during the locking period. The flow for clearing the SRAM is:

1. Requester releases lock
2. MCU SRAM starts clearing
3. MCU SRAM clearing ends
4. Mailbox is unlocked

The Requester is locked out of the mailbox after step 1, even though the lock isn't cleared until step 4.

It is expected that agents write their content from 0 to DLEN. If an agent writes outside of this SRAM area, there is no security guarantee for that content because that data would not be zeroized between mailbox operations.

**NOTE**: When DLEN = 0 the entire MBOX SRAM is cleared.

Document: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md
Section: Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Target User
Section text (lines 1315-1355):


A Target user is a
[trusted AXI user](#mcu-mailbox-limited-trusted-axi-users) that Root selects to
participate in a mailbox transaction. Root, typically MCU, is the only agent
that programs `TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_USER_VALID`.

Root shall write the Target AXI identity to `TARGET_USER` and then write
`TARGET_USER_VALID=1`. The numeric value in `TARGET_USER` has no ownership
meaning while valid is 0. 

While `TARGET_USER_VALID=0`, Root may write either target configuration
register. Writing `TARGET_USER_VALID=1` locks both registers against all
software writes. Software cannot retarget the mailbox or clear valid after the
grant. Hardware clears and unlocks both registers on a terminal
`TARGET_STATUS` write or when the mailbox is released.

One example of when a Target user becomes necessary is when the SOC wants
Caliptra to process a MBOX request. The SOC will obtain a lock, MCU will see the
command request is for Caliptra, MCU will program Caliptra as the Target user,
set `TARGET_USER_VALID`, and notify Caliptra.

Another example is when MCU itself obtains the mailbox lock. It will program a
Target user, set `TARGET_USER_VALID`, and notify the Target user via AXI or
some other mechanism.

A Target user has read access to the mailbox CSRs, and write access to:

- TARGET_STATUS register
- DLEN register and mailbox SRAM while it is the current [SRAM owner](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership)

The Target user shall finish all SRAM and DMA accesses before writing a
terminal `TARGET_STATUS` value, because that write ends its
[SRAM ownership](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership).

If a second Target user is required, MCU shall wait for the first Target to
publish a terminal `TARGET_STATUS` during normal operation. Hardware clears
`TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_USER_VALID` on that write, after which MCU can
program and validate the next Target user. `EXECUTE` remains 1 and the SRAM
contents are preserved, so a re-grant does not require releasing the mailbox.

Section: Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox SRAM Ownership
Section text (lines 1357-1416):


The SRAM owner is derived from mailbox state. Ownership is a combinational function of the mailbox
registers, evaluated in the following precedence order.

```mermaid
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: MCU mailbox SRAM owner resolution
    accDescr: A decision tree resolving the single exclusive SRAM owner from the lock, release, zeroization, EXECUTE, TARGET_USER_VALID, and CMD_STATUS state.

    Q1{"MBOX_LOCK set?"}
    Q2{"Releasing or SRAM zeroizing?"}
    Q3{"EXECUTE = 1?"}
    Q4{"TARGET_USER_VALID = 1?"}
    Q5{"CMD_STATUS = BUSY?"}

    NONE(["No software owner"])
    TGTO(["TARGET_USER agent"])
    ROOTO(["Root AXI user"])
    HOLD(["Lock holder"])

    Q1 -- No --> NONE
    Q1 -- Yes --> Q2
    Q2 -- Yes --> NONE
    Q2 -- No --> Q3
    Q3 -- No --> HOLD
    Q3 -- Yes --> Q4
    Q4 -- No --> Q5
    Q4 -- Yes --> TGTO
    Q5 -- No --> HOLD
    Q5 -- Yes --> ROOTO
```

Because ownership is combinational, each register write below is what moves
the exclusive owner from one agent to the next.

| Event | New exclusive SRAM owner |
|---|---|
| MCI reset | Root, as the reset lock holder |
| `LOCK` read returns 0 | The reading agent becomes lock holder |
| `EXECUTE=1` while `TARGET_USER_VALID=0` | Root |
| Root writes `TARGET_USER_VALID=1` while `EXECUTE=1` | The agent named by `TARGET_USER` |
| Target writes terminal `TARGET_STATUS` | Root, and hardware clears `TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_USER_VALID` |
| MCU writes non-BUSY `CMD_STATUS` | Lock holder |
| SRAM owner writes `EXECUTE=0` | None, and hardware begins zeroization |
| Zeroization completes | None, `LOCK` clears and the mailbox is reusable |

Writing `EXECUTE=0` revokes all software SRAM access and enters zeroization.

`CMD`, `DLEN` and `EXECUTE` write access follows SRAM ownership. Only the
current SRAM owner may write them, and writes from any other agent are dropped.
The agent that produced the data in the SRAM is the agent that reports its
length. The Requester cannot change or abort a request once `EXECUTE=1` hands
it to Root, while Root or a Target can end the transaction with `EXECUTE=0`
while it owns the SRAM.

**NOTE**: Neither the Requester nor Root can reclaim the mailbox from a Target
that never writes a terminal `TARGET_STATUS` or `EXECUTE=0`. Only an MCI reset
recovers it.

Section: MCI > Programming interface > MCU Mailbox
Section text (lines 2277-2290):


Each mailbox can be used for secure and restricted communication between external SoC entities, the MCU, and Caliptra core.  This communication channel is essential for exchanging control messages, status updates, and other critical information that the MCU will use to monitor system boot, firmware updates, and security critical operations. Mailboxes are designed to ensure that only authorized entities can access and communicate through it, preserving the integrity and security of the SoC operations.

The mailboxes are generic with some specific protocols and legal operations/accesses to ensure their secured and restricted aspect. The command, statuses, and data that are intepreted by the MCU microcontroller (uC), Caliptra uC or other SoC agent are not defined or enforced in this specification.

The MCU uC can function as an intermediary between agents such as Caliptra uC
and other SoC agents. MCU MBOX SRAM has one exclusive owner at a time, and MCU
accesses the SRAM only while it is that owner. See
[MCU Mailbox MCU Access](./CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md#mcu-mailbox-mcu-access)
for the MCU CSR access rules used by the flows below. Software can observe the
current owner through `MBOX_HW_STATUS.SRAM_OWNER`.

The [Caliptra SS HW MCU Mailbox Spec](./CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md#mcu-mailbox) has more details about the specific registers and interrupts used in the mailbox flows.

The Target may be a SOC agent or the Caliptra AXI user used for external
staging DMA.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: SOC sender routed through MCU to a target
    accDescr: Exclusive SRAM ownership moves from a SOC sender to the root agent, typically MCU, to a selected target, back to the root agent, and finally to the original sender.
    autonumber
    participant REQ as SOC Requester
    participant MBOX as MCU MBOX
    participant MCU
    participant TGT as SOC or Caliptra Target

    REQ->>MBOX: Read LOCK and stage SRAM, DLEN, CMD
    Note over REQ,MBOX: owner=SOC Requester
    REQ->>MBOX: Write EXECUTE=1
    Note over MCU,MBOX: owner=ROOT (MCU)
    MBOX-)MCU: notif_mbox*_cmd_avail interrupt
    MCU->>MBOX: Validate command, range, and target identity
    MCU->>MBOX: Write TARGET_USER=TGT
    MCU->>MBOX: Write TARGET_USER_VALID=1
    Note over MBOX,TGT: owner=Target
    MCU->>TGT: Sideband notification, for example a Caliptra mailbox command
    Note over MBOX,TGT: No MCU MBOX interrupt or data-avail wire asserts here
    TGT->>MBOX: Process or update SRAM and DLEN
    TGT->>MBOX: Write terminal TARGET_STATUS
    Note over MCU,MBOX: owner=ROOT (MCU). HW clears TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID
    MBOX-)MCU: notif_mbox*_target_done interrupt
    MCU->>MBOX: Read TARGET_STATUS and finalize response
    MCU->>MBOX: Write non-BUSY CMD_STATUS
    Note over REQ,MBOX: owner=SOC Requester
    REQ->>MBOX: Read CMD_STATUS and response
    REQ->>MBOX: Write EXECUTE=0
    Note over MBOX: SRAM zeroizes through maximum DLEN, then LOCK clears
```

`TARGET_STATUS` and `CMD_STATUS` are
[separate handshakes](./CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md#mcu-mailbox-status-registers).
The Requester regains ownership only after MCU writes non-BUSY `CMD_STATUS`.

Because the SOC Requester holds the lock in this flow, the
`cptra_ss_soc_mcu_mbox*_data_avail` wire stays deasserted when MCU programs
the target configuration. The Target learns that it owns the SRAM only through
the sideband notification, so MCU shall write `TARGET_USER`, set
`TARGET_USER_VALID`, and then send the notification.

    };

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

cases.summary: Smoke test that acquires an MCU mailbox lock over AXI DMA, reads the USER register, then writes the command, data length, 16 data words and the execute register. The only failure path is a lock that is never acquired.
intent: // Checking MBOX USER INFO
Smoke Test MCI MBOX%x  !!

stimulus.text: Select mailbox 1 when the valid vector is 0x2, otherwise mailbox 0.
Poll the mailbox lock register up to 32 times until the lock is acquired.
Read the mailbox USER register.
Write command 0xDEADBEEF to the mailbox CMD register.
Write the data length (16*4) to the DLEN register.
Write 16 data words into the mailbox SRAM.
Write 1 to the EXECUTE register.

checks.text: The lock acquisition succeeds only when the LOCK bit reads 0 within 32 attempts. Otherwise a FATAL message is printed, stdout control 0x1 is sent and the test hangs.

intent: Smoke Test MCI MBOX%x

EXECUTE must be seen set within 300 attempts; a timeout makes the returned fail nonzero, which main then checks.

stimulus.text: Boot MCU and Caliptra.

Run one aborted transaction per owned phase in random order with random terminal status.

tests.name: smoke_test_mcu_mbox_target_user

tests.name: smoke_test_mcu_mbox_valid_user

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will
                decrement immediately on being set - resulting in a pulse";

        default hw = w;
        default sw = r; // Has to have some access.... ideally SW wouldn't even see this
        default hwset = true;
        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Pulse mirrors interrupt event occurrence"; swwel = false;} pulse = 1'b0;
    };

    /* ---- Interrupt Statistics Counter ---- */
    reg intr_count_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Counter";
        desc = "Provides statistics about the number of events that have
                occurred.
                Will not overflow ('incrsaturate').";

        default sw = rw;
        default hw = na;
        default incrvalue = 1;
        default incrsaturate = true;
        default counter;

        field {desc = "Count field";} cnt[32] = 32'h0;
    };

Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md > Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox SRAM Clearing (lines 1461-1474)


When the mailbox lock is released the SRAM is zeroed out from 0 to max DLEN set during the locking period. The flow for clearing the SRAM is:

1. Requester releases lock
2. MCU SRAM starts clearing
3. MCU SRAM clearing ends
4. Mailbox is unlocked

The Requester is locked out of the mailbox after step 1, even though the lock isn't cleared until step 4.

It is expected that agents write their content from 0 to DLEN. If an agent writes outside of this SRAM area, there is no security guarantee for that content because that data would not be zeroized between mailbox operations.

**NOTE**: When DLEN = 0 the entire MBOX SRAM is cleared.


Requirements:

[r1] statement: The requester is locked out of the mailbox after releasing the lock (step 1), before the lock is cleared in step 4.  (aspect: access_control)
  q1 docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md L1469: The Requester is locked out of the mailbox after step 1, even though the lock isn't cleared until step 4.

[r2] statement: On lock release, the mailbox SRAM is zeroed from 0 to the max DLEN set during the locking period.  (aspect: functional)
  q1 docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md L1462: When the mailbox lock is released the SRAM is zeroed out from 0 to max DLEN set during the locking period.

relations.rationale: Raises DLEN while locked, then lowers it, executes, clears execute and re-acquires the lock. It then checks every SRAM dword up to the max DLEN reads zero.
Stages SRAM patterns, sets DLEN, releases the mailbox and re-acquires the lock. It then checks the wiped words read 0, and that the last word is zeroed only when DLEN reaches the SRAM size.
relations.missing: DLEN is set only once, so a max DLEN built up from several DLEN writes during the lock period is not exercised. Only 16 words plus the last word are sampled.

relations.rationale: After each transaction releases and re-acquires the lock, it checks that every SRAM word used reads 0.
relations.missing: Does not check the wipe boundary against the max DLEN, and does not exercise varying DLEN during the lock period.

relations.rationale: Writes random SRAM locations while tracking max DLEN, then writes DLEN, clears execute and re-acquires the lock. It checks the written locations read 0, including the full-size DLEN case at the max address.
relations.missing: Does not check that SRAM beyond the max DLEN is left untouched, and does not check the exact wiped range.

relations.rationale: Plan item states that SRAM is cleared on every lock release up to the max DLEN set during the lock.

In the release race, the Requester reads SRAM word 0 after a delay while the ender releases. It checks the read returns 0, which is consistent with lock-out during clearing.
relations.missing: Only a Requester SRAM read is checked. Writes and CSR accesses during clearing are not checked, and the lock-out is not tied explicitly to the interval before unlock.

relations.rationale: Writes SRAM while holding the lock and varies DLEN up then down. It then executes, clears the execute bit, re-acquires the lock, and checks every SRAM dword up to the max DLEN reads zero.
The plan item releases the lock and checks that SRAM is cleared up to the max DLEN set during lock.
Writes random SRAM locations while tracking max DLEN, then releases via a DLEN write, execute clear and lock re-acquire. It checks that the written locations read 0.
relations.missing: Only sampled written locations are checked. The full range 0x0 to max DLEN is not checked, and nothing checks that the clear stops at max DLEN.

relations.rationale: After release and lock re-acquire, the SRAM words the transaction used are read as 0, which shows a wipe.
relations.missing: Only the payload words used are checked, not the whole range from 0x0 to max DLEN. The relation between the cleared range and the max DLEN is not verified.

relations.rationale: Walks the Requester, Root, Target, Root, Requester ownership transitions, including terminal statuses and aborts. At each phase it checks that the HW_STATUS SRAM owner matches the expected owner.
Checks that the SRAM owner is Root after the requester sets EXECUTE, and Target after TARGET_USER_VALID is written and CMD_STATUS is set.
relations.missing: The Requester-owner case and the dependence on CMD_STATUS and LOCK transitions are not verified. Only two owner states are checked.

relations.rationale: Grants SRAM ownership to the target by writing TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID after EXECUTE. It checks the access consequences before and after the grant.
relations.missing: The SRAM owner value is never read or checked. Ownership derivation from LOCK, EXECUTE and CMD_STATUS is not verified.

relations.rationale: At each phase non-owner agents read 0 and their writes are dropped, while the owner still reads its own payload. The release race is also covered.
A non-owner target reads 0 and its writes are dropped before the grant. The MCU as non-owner also has its SRAM write attempts checked after the target is granted.
relations.missing: Only some owner and non-owner combinations are exercised, not every ownership phase such as the requester or Root owner. Reads by other agents are not checked.

relations.rationale: Without the lock, SRAM reads return 0 and a write attempt is dropped (SRAM dword 5 still reads 0).
relations.missing: Only the no-lock (non-owner) case is checked. Owner access and other ownership phases are not verified.

relations.rationale: A user without the lock reads 0 from SRAM and a write attempt is dropped (SRAM dword 5 still reads 0).
relations.missing: Only the non-owner without-lock case is checked, not other ownership phases or non-owner access in every state.

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the

                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse

    reg intr_count_incr_t {
        name = "Interrupt Event Count Incrementor";
        desc = "Trigger the event counter to increment based on observing
                the rising edge of an interrupt event input from the
                Hardware. The same input signal that causes an interrupt
                event to be set (sticky) also causes this signal to pulse
                for 1 clock cycle, resulting in the event counter
                incrementing by 1 for every interrupt event.
                This is implemented as a down-counter (1-bit) that will

        default decrvalue = 1;
        default counter;

    };

relations.rationale: Writes TARGET_USER bytes while TARGET_USER_VALID is 0 and reads them back. It then sets valid, tries to write 0, and checks that TARGET_USER keeps its previous value.
Root writes TARGET_USER before TARGET_USER_VALID is set and the value reads back.
relations.missing: No check that a write is blocked once TARGET_USER_VALID is set, and no check that non-Root writers are rejected.

relations.rationale: Writes TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID and reads the user value back, so a write while valid is 0 is shown to work.
relations.missing: No attempt to write TARGET_USER while TARGET_USER_VALID is 1, and no non-Root write attempt.

relations.rationale: A non-owner Target attempts to write TARGET_USER after the grant and the value stays unchanged.
relations.missing: Root writes while valid is 0 (allowed) and while valid is 1 (blocked) are not checked. The tested writer is a non-Root agent.

relations.rationale: After TARGET_USER_VALID is set, a write to TARGET_USER is attempted and ignored.
relations.missing: The lock on the TARGET_USER_VALID register itself and the hardware clear that releases the lock are not verified.

relations.rationale: Writes to TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID are attempted by a non-owner after the grant and both stay unchanged. Hardware then clears TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID after the terminal status.
relations.missing: The attempted writes come from the Target, not from Root, so the Root-lock case is not verified.

relations.rationale: Clears EXECUTE to release the mailbox directly and then checks that TARGET_USER reads 0.
Releases the lock and checks that all CSRs are 0, which includes TARGET_USER.
The plan item states that the target user is valid only when TARGET_USER_VALID is set.
The target publishes a COMPLETE terminal status and TARGET_USER then reads 0 after hardware clears it.
relations.missing: Only the COMPLETE terminal status is exercised. The other terminal statuses and abort paths are not checked for the clear.

relations.rationale: A TARGET_USER write takes effect while TARGET_USER_VALID is 0 and is ignored after valid is set.
relations.missing: target_cfg_write_en is not observed directly, and the Root-only condition is not exercised with a non-Root writer.

relations.rationale: A non-owner Target's write to TARGET_USER is dropped after the grant.
relations.missing: The case where the write is enabled is not verified, and neither is the dependence on target_cfg_write_en.

relations.rationale: After the terminal target status, TARGET_USER reads 0 again, so hardware cleared the field.

relations.rationale: Runs full transactions and aborts in each owned phase, with Root writing a non-BUSY CMD_STATUS. It checks the HW_STATUS SRAM owner in each phase and that the Requester owns the mailbox again at the end.

Root writes CMD_STATUS=COMPLETE (a terminal value) while the Target owns the SRAM. The test expects the SRAM owner to stay Target afterwards, but the requirement says a terminal write returns ownership to the Requester.
Root writes CMD_COMPLETE to CMD_STATUS and reads it back as COMPLETE, which checks the encoding of the value.
relations.missing: The meaning of the value is not checked: no scenario shows a completed command and no consumer reacts to it.

relations.rationale: The MCU sets DATA_READY and the requester polls until it reads DATA_READY. It then verifies the response data and DLEN.
relations.missing: The status is only waited for, with no check of the status register value outside the helper. The data-ready meaning is shown only through the data read-back.

relations.rationale: The MCU sets CMD_STATUS to DATA_READY and the test checks that it reads DATA_READY while the data is read back.
relations.missing: Only the encoded value is checked; the meaning of the value beyond the data read-back is not verified.

relations.rationale: The test polls CMD_STATUS until it reads 0x2 (complete) after EXECUTE is set.
relations.missing: Only the value 0x2 is awaited; no check of the meaning beyond the polling.

relations.rationale: MCU writes status 0x2 and the Caliptra side polls CMD_STATUS until it reads complete.
relations.missing: Only the encoding and the polling for it are checked; nothing further verifies the meaning of the complete state.

relations.rationale: The SoC agent polls CMD_STATUS until it reads complete after sending the command.
relations.missing: Only waits for the value with a timeout; no other check of the meaning of the complete state.

relations.rationale: The test waits for CMD_STATUS to report complete (0x2) as a sync point.
relations.missing: Only waits for the value; no further verification of the meaning of the complete state.

relations.rationale: Writes CMD_STATUS=DATA_READY with an 8-bit write and checks that it reads back DATA_READY.
relations.missing: Only the register value is checked; the meaning of the status is not exercised.

relations.rationale: MCU writes CMD_STATUS=DATA_READY and the test checks it reads back DATA_READY and is unchanged after the target's blocked write attempts.
relations.missing: Only the encoded value is checked; the meaning of the status is not exercised.

relations.rationale: CMD_STATUS is written and read back, then reads 0 after EXECUTE is cleared and the mailbox is released. This shows the hardware clears the field.
A non-owner attempts to write CMD_STATUS and the test checks the value is not taken.
relations.missing: Only a non-owner target write is tried; writes by other agents such as the Requester are not checked, nor that the MCU write succeeds.

relations.rationale: A USER write to CMD_STATUS must not take effect, checked both while the user holds the lock and after the MCU takes over.

relations.rationale: A user without the lock tries to write CMD_STATUS and the readback must not show the written value.

request:
Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md > Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Locking (lines 1304-1313)


A Requester will read the "LOCK" register to obtain a lock on the mailbox. This is a read-set register, the lock is acquired when read returns 0. The Requester must be a [Trusted user](#mcu-mailbox-limited-trusted-axi-users). Once the lock is obtained the Requester has read access to the mailbox CSRs and, while the Requester is the current [SRAM owner](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership), write access to:

- CMD, DLEN and EXECUTE registers
- mailbox SRAM

Unlocking/releasing occurs when the current SRAM owner writes 0 to the EXECUTE register. The Requester can release only while it owns the SRAM: before it writes `EXECUTE=1`, or after ownership returns to it. Once `EXECUTE=1` hands the SRAM to Root, the Requester cannot abort the transaction. After releasing the mailbox the SRAM is zeroed out([MCU Mailbox SRAM Clearing](#mcu-mailbox-sram-clearing)).

On MCI reset release the MCU MBOX is locked for MCU. The MCU shall set the DLEN to the size of the SRAM and release the MBOX, causing the SRAM to be zeroed. This is done to prevent data leaking between warm resets via the SRAM.


Requirements:

[r1] statement: Once locked, the Requester has read access to the mailbox CSRs.  (aspect: access_control)
  q1 docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md L1305: Once the lock is obtained the Requester has read access to the mailbox CSRs

[r2] statement: After the mailbox is released, the SRAM is zeroed out.  (aspect: functional)
  q1 docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md L1310: After releasing the mailbox the SRAM is zeroed out([MCU Mailbox SRAM Clearing](#mcu-mailbox-sram-clearing)).

relations.rationale: After TARGET_USER_VALID is set by an 8-bit write, the test tries to write 0 to TARGET_USER and checks that TARGET_USER keeps its previous value. That shows Root target configuration writes are blocked while valid is set.
relations.missing: Only TARGET_USER is checked. A write to TARGET_USER_VALID while it is set is not attempted, and the deassertion of target_cfg_write_en is not observed directly.

relations.rationale: A non-owner target attempts writes to EXECUTE, DLEN and CMD and the test checks they are dropped. When the writer is the owner (can_write), DLEN and CMD must take the written value.
relations.missing: The owner's EXECUTE write is not checked as succeeding. The blocking is shown only for a Target agent in the pre-grant phase.

relations.rationale: Root writes DLEN and CMD while it owns the SRAM and they take effect. After the grant to the Target, Root's CMD write is dropped and its EXECUTE clear is ignored.
relations.missing: A Root DLEN write while the Target owns the SRAM is not checked. An EXECUTE write while Root owns the SRAM is not checked as succeeding.

relations.rationale: The Caliptra uC writes CMD, DLEN and EXECUTE as the owner. The MCU, as a non-owner, then attempts writes to EXECUTE, DLEN and CMD and the test checks they are dropped.
relations.missing: The owner-side writes are not checked directly through read-back. The blocked-write checks cover only the MCU non-owner case after EXECUTE is set.

relations.rationale: A Caliptra uC without the lock attempts writes to EXECUTE, DLEN and CMD and the test checks they do not take effect.
relations.missing: Writes succeeding for the current SRAM owner are not checked. Only a non-owner without the lock is exercised, not the owner-gating after EXECUTE.

relations.rationale: The plan item intends to check that the requester has write permission to SRAM, CMD, DLEN and EXECUTE.
relations.missing: No check that these writes are blocked for a non-owner, which is the gating behavior.

There are 2 mailboxes in the MCI. Each Mailbox component of the MCI allows for secure and restricted communication between external SoC entities and the MCU. This communication channel is essential for exchanging control messages, status updates, and other critical information that the MCU will use to monitor system boot, firmware updates, and security critical operations. Mailboxes are designed to ensure that only authorized entities can access and communicate through it, preserving the integrity and security of the SoC operations.

request:
Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSIntegrationSpecification.md > MCI > Programming interface > MCU Mailbox > SOC Requester to SOC Target Communication Flow (MCU as intermediary) (lines 2377-2423)


The Target may be a SOC agent or the Caliptra AXI user used for external
staging DMA.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: SOC sender routed through MCU to a target
    accDescr: Exclusive SRAM ownership moves from a SOC sender to the root agent, typically MCU, to a selected target, back to the root agent, and finally to the original sender.
    autonumber
    participant REQ as SOC Requester
    participant MBOX as MCU MBOX
    participant MCU
    participant TGT as SOC or Caliptra Target

    REQ->>MBOX: Read LOCK and stage SRAM, DLEN, CMD
    Note over REQ,MBOX: owner=SOC Requester
    REQ->>MBOX: Write EXECUTE=1
    Note over MCU,MBOX: owner=ROOT (MCU)
    MBOX-)MCU: notif_mbox*_cmd_avail interrupt
    MCU->>MBOX: Validate command, range, and target identity
    MCU->>MBOX: Write TARGET_USER=TGT
    MCU->>MBOX: Write TARGET_USER_VALID=1
    Note over MBOX,TGT: owner=Target
    MCU->>TGT: Sideband notification, for example a Caliptra mailbox command
    Note over MBOX,TGT: No MCU MBOX interrupt or data-avail wire asserts here
    TGT->>MBOX: Process or update SRAM and DLEN
    TGT->>MBOX: Write terminal TARGET_STATUS
    Note over MCU,MBOX: owner=ROOT (MCU). HW clears TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID
    MBOX-)MCU: notif_mbox*_target_done interrupt
    MCU->>MBOX: Read TARGET_STATUS and finalize response
    MCU->>MBOX: Write non-BUSY CMD_STATUS
    Note over REQ,MBOX: owner=SOC Requester
    REQ->>MBOX: Read CMD_STATUS and response
    REQ->>MBOX: Write EXECUTE=0
    Note over MBOX: SRAM zeroizes through maximum DLEN, then LOCK clears
```

`TARGET_STATUS` and `CMD_STATUS` are
[separate handshakes](./CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md#mcu-mailbox-status-registers).
The Requester regains ownership only after MCU writes non-BUSY `CMD_STATUS`.

Because the SOC Requester holds the lock in this flow, the
`cptra_ss_soc_mcu_mbox*_data_avail` wire stays deasserted when MCU programs
the target configuration. The Target learns that it owns the SRAM only through
the sideband notification, so MCU shall write `TARGET_USER`, set
`TARGET_USER_VALID`, and then send the notification.


Requirements:

[r1] statement: MCU writes TARGET_USER, sets TARGET_USER_VALID, and only then sends the sideband notification.  (aspect: functional)
  q1 docs/CaliptraSSIntegrationSpecification.md L2421: so MCU shall write `TARGET_USER`, set
  q2 docs/CaliptraSSIntegrationSpecification.md L2422: `TARGET_USER_VALID`, and then send the notification.

  summary: Checks that the target done interrupt is set when the TARGET_DONE register is set.
  stimulus:
    s1 Set the TARGET_DONE register.
  checks:
    k1 [failure handling unknown] Target done interrupt is set.

Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSIntegrationSpecification.md > MCI > Programming interface > MCU Mailbox > SOC Requester to SOC Target Communication Flow (MCU as intermediary) (lines 2377-2423)


The Target may be a SOC agent or the Caliptra AXI user used for external
staging DMA.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: SOC sender routed through MCU to a target
    accDescr: Exclusive SRAM ownership moves from a SOC sender to the root agent, typically MCU, to a selected target, back to the root agent, and finally to the original sender.
    autonumber
    participant REQ as SOC Requester
    participant MBOX as MCU MBOX
    participant MCU
    participant TGT as SOC or Caliptra Target

    REQ->>MBOX: Read LOCK and stage SRAM, DLEN, CMD
    Note over REQ,MBOX: owner=SOC Requester
    REQ->>MBOX: Write EXECUTE=1
    Note over MCU,MBOX: owner=ROOT (MCU)
    MBOX-)MCU: notif_mbox*_cmd_avail interrupt
    MCU->>MBOX: Validate command, range, and target identity
    MCU->>MBOX: Write TARGET_USER=TGT
    MCU->>MBOX: Write TARGET_USER_VALID=1
    Note over MBOX,TGT: owner=Target
    MCU->>TGT: Sideband notification, for example a Caliptra mailbox command
    Note over MBOX,TGT: No MCU MBOX interrupt or data-avail wire asserts here
    TGT->>MBOX: Process or update SRAM and DLEN
    TGT->>MBOX: Write terminal TARGET_STATUS
    Note over MCU,MBOX: owner=ROOT (MCU). HW clears TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID
    MBOX-)MCU: notif_mbox*_target_done interrupt
    MCU->>MBOX: Read TARGET_STATUS and finalize response
    MCU->>MBOX: Write non-BUSY CMD_STATUS
    Note over REQ,MBOX: owner=SOC Requester
    REQ->>MBOX: Read CMD_STATUS and response
    REQ->>MBOX: Write EXECUTE=0
    Note over MBOX: SRAM zeroizes through maximum DLEN, then LOCK clears
```

`TARGET_STATUS` and `CMD_STATUS` are
[separate handshakes](./CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md#mcu-mailbox-status-registers).
The Requester regains ownership only after MCU writes non-BUSY `CMD_STATUS`.

Because the SOC Requester holds the lock in this flow, the
`cptra_ss_soc_mcu_mbox*_data_avail` wire stays deasserted when MCU programs
the target configuration. The Target learns that it owns the SRAM only through
the sideband notification, so MCU shall write `TARGET_USER`, set
`TARGET_USER_VALID`, and then send the notification.

relations.rationale: After release by EXECUTE=0 and LOCK re-acquire, every SRAM word the transaction used reads 0.
relations.missing: The maximum DLEN is not varied or checked, only the words used by the transaction are read, and the LOCK clearing is not checked explicitly.

relations.rationale: Writes DLEN, clears EXECUTE, re-acquires the lock, and checks the 10 burst-written locations read zero.

relations.rationale: MCU waits for the target's COMPLETE TARGET_STATUS and clears the target done interrupt.

relations.rationale: Root sets TARGET_USER_VALID=1 and the test checks the HW_STATUS SRAM owner and the owner's SRAM access per phase.

MCU writes TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID and the target then writes SRAM, DLEN and CMD successfully, while before the grant its writes are dropped.
relations.missing: The SRAM owner status is not checked explicitly, only the ownership effect through access.

Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSIntegrationSpecification.md > MCI > Programming interface > MCU Mailbox > SOC Requester to SOC Target Communication Flow (MCU as intermediary) (lines 2377-2423)


The Target may be a SOC agent or the Caliptra AXI user used for external
staging DMA.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: SOC sender routed through MCU to a target
    accDescr: Exclusive SRAM ownership moves from a SOC sender to the root agent, typically MCU, to a selected target, back to the root agent, and finally to the original sender.
    autonumber
    participant REQ as SOC Requester
    participant MBOX as MCU MBOX
    participant MCU
    participant TGT as SOC or Caliptra Target

    REQ->>MBOX: Read LOCK and stage SRAM, DLEN, CMD
    Note over REQ,MBOX: owner=SOC Requester
    REQ->>MBOX: Write EXECUTE=1
    Note over MCU,MBOX: owner=ROOT (MCU)
    MBOX-)MCU: notif_mbox*_cmd_avail interrupt
    MCU->>MBOX: Validate command, range, and target identity
    MCU->>MBOX: Write TARGET_USER=TGT
    MCU->>MBOX: Write TARGET_USER_VALID=1
    Note over MBOX,TGT: owner=Target
    MCU->>TGT: Sideband notification, for example a Caliptra mailbox command
    Note over MBOX,TGT: No MCU MBOX interrupt or data-avail wire asserts here
    TGT->>MBOX: Process or update SRAM and DLEN
    TGT->>MBOX: Write terminal TARGET_STATUS
    Note over MCU,MBOX: owner=ROOT (MCU). HW clears TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID
    MBOX-)MCU: notif_mbox*_target_done interrupt
    MCU->>MBOX: Read TARGET_STATUS and finalize response
    MCU->>MBOX: Write non-BUSY CMD_STATUS
    Note over REQ,MBOX: owner=SOC Requester
    REQ->>MBOX: Read CMD_STATUS and response
    REQ->>MBOX: Write EXECUTE=0
    Note over MBOX: SRAM zeroizes through maximum DLEN, then LOCK clears
```

`TARGET_STATUS` and `CMD_STATUS` are
[separate handshakes](./CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md#mcu-mailbox-status-registers).
The Requester regains ownership only after MCU writes non-BUSY `CMD_STATUS`.

Because the SOC Requester holds the lock in this flow, the
`cptra_ss_soc_mcu_mbox*_data_avail` wire stays deasserted when MCU programs
the target configuration. The Target learns that it owns the SRAM only through
the sideband notification, so MCU shall write `TARGET_USER`, set
`TARGET_USER_VALID`, and then send the notification.

Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md > Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Status Registers (lines 1418-1447)


`CMD_STATUS` and `TARGET_STATUS` use the following encodings:

| Value | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 0 | BUSY |
| 1 | DATA_READY |
| 2 | COMPLETE |
| 3 | FAILURE |

The two status registers serve different polling domains. Only MCU writes
`CMD_STATUS`, and the original Requester polls it. Only the current Target
writes `TARGET_STATUS`, and MCU reads it. A terminal Target status shall not be
visible as command completion to the original Requester until MCU separately
writes a terminal `CMD_STATUS`.

Hardware resets `TARGET_STATUS` to BUSY on each Target handoff.

`CMD_STATUS` is not used when MCU is the Requester, because there is no
external Requester to serve. In that case MCU reads `TARGET_STATUS` directly.

`MBOX_HW_STATUS.SRAM_OWNER` reports the current exclusive SRAM owner:

| Value | Owner |
|---:|---|
| 0 | None |
| 1 | Requester/lock holder |
| 2 | Root AXI user, typically MCU |
| 3 | Target selected by `TARGET_USER` while `TARGET_USER_VALID=1` |

Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md > Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Locking (lines 1304-1313)


A Requester will read the "LOCK" register to obtain a lock on the mailbox. This is a read-set register, the lock is acquired when read returns 0. The Requester must be a [Trusted user](#mcu-mailbox-limited-trusted-axi-users). Once the lock is obtained the Requester has read access to the mailbox CSRs and, while the Requester is the current [SRAM owner](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership), write access to:

- CMD, DLEN and EXECUTE registers
- mailbox SRAM

Unlocking/releasing occurs when the current SRAM owner writes 0 to the EXECUTE register. The Requester can release only while it owns the SRAM: before it writes `EXECUTE=1`, or after ownership returns to it. Once `EXECUTE=1` hands the SRAM to Root, the Requester cannot abort the transaction. After releasing the mailbox the SRAM is zeroed out([MCU Mailbox SRAM Clearing](#mcu-mailbox-sram-clearing)).

On MCI reset release the MCU MBOX is locked for MCU. The MCU shall set the DLEN to the size of the SRAM and release the MBOX, causing the SRAM to be zeroed. This is done to prevent data leaking between warm resets via the SRAM.

`CMD_STATUS` and `TARGET_STATUS` use the following encodings:

| Value | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 0 | BUSY |
| 1 | DATA_READY |
| 2 | COMPLETE |
| 3 | FAILURE |

The two status registers serve different polling domains. Only MCU writes
`CMD_STATUS`, and the original Requester polls it. Only the current Target
writes `TARGET_STATUS`, and MCU reads it. A terminal Target status shall not be
visible as command completion to the original Requester until MCU separately
writes a terminal `CMD_STATUS`.

Hardware resets `TARGET_STATUS` to BUSY on each Target handoff.

`CMD_STATUS` is not used when MCU is the Requester, because there is no
external Requester to serve. In that case MCU reads `TARGET_STATUS` directly.

`MBOX_HW_STATUS.SRAM_OWNER` reports the current exclusive SRAM owner:

| Value | Owner |
|---:|---|
| 0 | None |
| 1 | Requester/lock holder |
| 2 | Root AXI user, typically MCU |
| 3 | Target selected by `TARGET_USER` while `TARGET_USER_VALID=1` |

relations.rationale: The target publishes a COMPLETE terminal TARGET_STATUS after Root sets TARGET_USER_VALID. The test then reads TARGET_USER_VALID and requires 0 (hardware clear).
After Root sets TARGET_USER_VALID and the target completes, the test checks that the field reads 0 with no software write, which shows hardware cleared it.
A Root write to TARGET_USER_VALID is accepted. A non-owner target write attempt while the field is 0 leaves it unchanged.

relations.rationale: After writing TARGET_USER_VALID=1, the test clears EXECUTE to release the mailbox and checks that the field reads 0.

Root writes TARGET_USER_VALID=1 with an 8-bit write and it reads back 1.
relations.missing: Rejection of non-Root writes and of Root writes while the field is already 1 is not checked.

relations.rationale: After valid is set, a write of 0 to TARGET_USER is attempted and TARGET_USER keeps its value, which shows TARGET_USER is locked.

Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md > Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Limited Trusted AXI users (lines 1296-1302)


There are 5 trusted AXI Users determined at build time via parameters or via MCI lockable registers. These users, a default user 0xFFFF_FFFF, and MCU are the only AXI users that can access or obtain a lock on the mailbox.

Any untrusted AXI user trying to read or write the mailbox will receive an AXI error response ([MCU Mailbox Errors](#mcu-mailbox-errors)).

Trusted users always have read access to the CSRs in the mailbox, but require MBOX [lock](#mcu-mailbox-locking) to write the CSRs. SRAM reads and writes require the trusted user to be the current [exclusive SRAM owner](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership).

relations.rationale: The Caliptra uC is configured with an invalid AXI user, then writes and reads every mailbox CSR and random SRAM addresses. Each access must return an AXI error.

Writes and reads of every mailbox CSR and random SRAM addresses are checked to return an AXI error, and the checks are worded as 'invalid user'. The scenario is described as a mailbox that is not instantiated.
relations.missing: It is not shown that the AXI error comes from an untrusted user on an instantiated mailbox rather than from the mailbox being absent.

relations.rationale: The Caliptra uC reads and writes several CSRs and SRAM and checks for an AXI error when it is not a trusted user under the parameterised configuration.
relations.missing: Only some CSRs are covered (EXECUTE, CMD, CMD_STATUS, USER, LOCK, DLEN). The error is expected only in the non-param configuration.

relations.rationale: The plan item states that AXI accesses from invalid users are rejected and report an AXI error.
Exercises the Caliptra uC AXI ID chosen either from a build-time parameter or from the CSR-configured valid users, and checks the resulting access or AXI error behaviour.
relations.missing: Does not verify that there are exactly 5 trusted users, nor that each of the five parameter and CSR slots is honored.

relations.rationale: Checks that the valid user parameters take effect only when the VALID parameter is set, which concerns the build-time parameter path.
relations.missing: The count of 5 users and the lockable-CSR path are not verified.

relations.rationale: Checks the interplay between the valid user parameters and the CSR, namely that the parameters take precedence.
relations.missing: The count of 5 trusted users is not verified, nor the CSR-lockable configuration on its own.

relations.rationale: Before ownership is granted, the non-owner target reads SRAM as 0 and its SRAM writes are dropped. After the grant, SRAM data is checked and the target writes SRAM.
Across the ownership phases, every non-owner agent reads the payload as 0 and the owner reads its data back after non-owner write attempts. HW_STATUS is checked against the expected owner.
A user that does not hold the lock reads SRAM as 0 and has its writes dropped.
relations.missing: Only the no-lock state is exercised. There is no check of SRAM owner transitions or of a trusted non-owner under an active lock.

relations.rationale: A user without the lock reads SRAM as 0, and its write attempts to SRAM are dropped.
relations.missing: The SRAM owner state is not checked. Only the no-lock case is covered, not the owner or non-owner phases.

relations.rationale: A valid user without permission, for example without the lock, accessing SRAM has its writes dropped and its reads return 0.
relations.missing: It does not tie the check to the exclusive SRAM owner, and it gives only an example.

relations.rationale: The target, a trusted user that holds no lock, reads CMD, MBOX USER, DLEN and CMD_STATUS, and the values are checked.
relations.missing: Only one trusted user is tested, and CSR reads are not checked across all lock states or for all CSRs.

relations.rationale: The plan item states that CSRs are readable by all valid users.
Without the lock, the Caliptra uC attempts writes to EXECUTE, DLEN, CMD, CMD_STATUS and USER. Each register is read back and must not take the written value.
The non-owner target, which holds no lock, attempts writes to the CSRs (DLEN, CMD, EXECUTE, CMD_STATUS, USER, TARGET_USER, TARGET_USER_VALID). The register values are checked to be unchanged.
relations.missing: The positive case, a user that holds the lock writing the CSRs, is not checked. Only one non-lock user is tested.

relations.rationale: A write attempt to CSRs without the lock is checked to leave EXECUTE, DLEN, CMD, CMD_STATUS and USER unchanged.
relations.missing: The lock-held write success is not verified. Only a subset of the CSRs is covered.

relations.rationale: A valid user lacking permission has its writes dropped silently.
relations.missing: It names only an SRAM example and does not specify CSR writes without the lock or a lock-held write.

relations.rationale: An untrusted user's accesses to all CSRs, including the LOCK CSR, and to SRAM return AXI errors.
relations.missing: Does not verify that the default user 0xFFFF_FFFF or MCU are allowed access, nor that trusted users can obtain the lock.

relations.rationale: Checks that DEFAULT_USER (all 1s) is treated as a valid user even when it is not explicitly configured.
relations.missing: Does not verify rejection of other users, nor MCU access or lock acquisition.

relations.rationale: Checks that a valid user can get a lock on a mailbox.
relations.missing: Does not verify that untrusted users cannot obtain the lock, nor the default user or MCU cases.

relations.rationale: Checks that the MCU can get a lock on a mailbox.
relations.missing: Does not verify the trusted-user or default-user cases, nor exclusion of untrusted users.

relations.rationale: The test sets then clears EXECUTE to start zeroization and reads LOCK while zeroization is in progress.
relations.missing: It does not check that the mailbox is released after the clear, i.e. wipe completion or the lock becoming free again. It only checks that LOCK reads 1 during zeroize.

relations.rationale: The owner releases the mailbox with EXECUTE=0, then the test checks that the SRAM words are wiped, that LOCK can be re-acquired and that the Requester owns the mailbox again.
Across the ownership phases, non-owner EXECUTE=0 writes are checked to be dropped (SRAM owner unchanged), while the current owner's EXECUTE=0 write takes effect and releases the mailbox.
Root tries to clear EXECUTE while the Target owns the SRAM and the test checks that EXECUTE stays set.
relations.missing: The positive case, a write by the valid SRAM owner taking effect on EXECUTE, is not checked.

relations.rationale: The test releases the mailbox by writing the execute register, then re-acquires LOCK and checks that the SRAM is wiped as expected.
The test clears execute after writing dlen, re-acquires the lock and checks that the written SRAM locations read 0 after release.
After the hand-off, a write to EXECUTE is attempted by a non-owner and the test checks that EXECUTE is not cleared.
relations.missing: The positive case, a write by the valid owner taking effect, is not checked.

relations.rationale: The Caliptra uC target is granted SRAM ownership and processes the MCU command. The test waits for the target to publish the COMPLETE terminal status in the target status register. It then checks the target done interrupt and the hardware clearing of TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID, so COMPLETE is observed as the target's command-complete outcome.

request:
Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md > Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Target User (lines 1315-1355)


A Target user is a
[trusted AXI user](#mcu-mailbox-limited-trusted-axi-users) that Root selects to
participate in a mailbox transaction. Root, typically MCU, is the only agent
that programs `TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_USER_VALID`.

Root shall write the Target AXI identity to `TARGET_USER` and then write
`TARGET_USER_VALID=1`. The numeric value in `TARGET_USER` has no ownership
meaning while valid is 0. 

While `TARGET_USER_VALID=0`, Root may write either target configuration
register. Writing `TARGET_USER_VALID=1` locks both registers against all
software writes. Software cannot retarget the mailbox or clear valid after the
grant. Hardware clears and unlocks both registers on a terminal
`TARGET_STATUS` write or when the mailbox is released.

One example of when a Target user becomes necessary is when the SOC wants
Caliptra to process a MBOX request. The SOC will obtain a lock, MCU will see the
command request is for Caliptra, MCU will program Caliptra as the Target user,
set `TARGET_USER_VALID`, and notify Caliptra.

Another example is when MCU itself obtains the mailbox lock. It will program a
Target user, set `TARGET_USER_VALID`, and notify the Target user via AXI or
some other mechanism.

A Target user has read access to the mailbox CSRs, and write access to:

- TARGET_STATUS register
- DLEN register and mailbox SRAM while it is the current [SRAM owner](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership)

The Target user shall finish all SRAM and DMA accesses before writing a
terminal `TARGET_STATUS` value, because that write ends its
[SRAM ownership](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership).

If a second Target user is required, MCU shall wait for the first Target to
publish a terminal `TARGET_STATUS` during normal operation. Hardware clears
`TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_USER_VALID` on that write, after which MCU can
program and validate the next Target user. `EXECUTE` remains 1 and the SRAM
contents are preserved, so a re-grant does not require releasing the mailbox.

request:
Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md > Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox Target User (lines 1315-1355)


A Target user is a
[trusted AXI user](#mcu-mailbox-limited-trusted-axi-users) that Root selects to
participate in a mailbox transaction. Root, typically MCU, is the only agent
that programs `TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_USER_VALID`.

Root shall write the Target AXI identity to `TARGET_USER` and then write
`TARGET_USER_VALID=1`. The numeric value in `TARGET_USER` has no ownership
meaning while valid is 0. 

While `TARGET_USER_VALID=0`, Root may write either target configuration
register. Writing `TARGET_USER_VALID=1` locks both registers against all
software writes. Software cannot retarget the mailbox or clear valid after the
grant. Hardware clears and unlocks both registers on a terminal
`TARGET_STATUS` write or when the mailbox is released.

One example of when a Target user becomes necessary is when the SOC wants
Caliptra to process a MBOX request. The SOC will obtain a lock, MCU will see the
command request is for Caliptra, MCU will program Caliptra as the Target user,
set `TARGET_USER_VALID`, and notify Caliptra.

Another example is when MCU itself obtains the mailbox lock. It will program a
Target user, set `TARGET_USER_VALID`, and notify the Target user via AXI or
some other mechanism.

A Target user has read access to the mailbox CSRs, and write access to:

- TARGET_STATUS register
- DLEN register and mailbox SRAM while it is the current [SRAM owner](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership)

The Target user shall finish all SRAM and DMA accesses before writing a
terminal `TARGET_STATUS` value, because that write ends its
[SRAM ownership](#mcu-mailbox-sram-ownership).

If a second Target user is required, MCU shall wait for the first Target to
publish a terminal `TARGET_STATUS` during normal operation. Hardware clears
`TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_USER_VALID` on that write, after which MCU can
program and validate the next Target user. `EXECUTE` remains 1 and the SRAM
contents are preserved, so a re-grant does not require releasing the mailbox.

relations.rationale: After the Target writes a terminal TARGET_STATUS, the test checks the HW_STATUS SRAM owner in each phase. It also checks that non-owners read 0 and the owner keeps its data, for normal and aborted transactions.
The target sets a terminal status and the test then reads SRAM data and CSRs after completion. It never directly checks that the SRAM owner changed.
relations.missing: No direct check that SRAM ownership ended; the HW_STATUS check masks out the SRAM_OWNER bit.

relations.rationale: The test grants TARGET_USER and TARGET_USER_VALID, waits for the target's COMPLETE status, and checks that TARGET_USER_VALID and TARGET_USER read 0 afterwards.
The target writes a terminal status after the grant and the test sees it. Before the grant the target's CSR writes are checked as dropped, but TARGET_STATUS is not among the registers attempted.
relations.missing: No attempt to write TARGET_STATUS while valid_target_req is deasserted (e.g. before the grant) to show the write is ignored.

relations.rationale: A non-target agent's 8-bit write to TARGET_STATUS is checked as having no effect. This covers only the blocked side of the gating.
relations.missing: The write succeeding when valid_target_req is asserted is not exercised, and the gating signal is not tied to the blocked write.

relations.rationale: Root's write to TARGET_STATUS is checked as having no effect. This covers only the blocked side of the gating.
relations.missing: The write taking effect when valid_target_req is asserted is not exercised.

relations.rationale: The target publishes a COMPLETE status. The test checks that the target done interrupt is set and then clears it, which verifies that Root is notified.
The Target writes a terminal TARGET_STATUS and the test waits for TARGET_DONE. No check asserts the notification itself; only the final error-count check applies.
relations.missing: No explicit check that the notification is raised or for its timing.

relations.rationale: Plans to check that SRAM is cleared on lock release up to the max DLEN set during lock. This covers the general clearing behavior.
relations.missing: Does not address DLEN = 0 or that the entire SRAM is erased in that case. It describes clearing only up to the max DLEN.

Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md > Manufacturer Control Interface (MCI) > MCI Feature Descriptions > MCU Mailbox > MCU Mailbox SRAM Ownership (lines 1357-1416)


The SRAM owner is derived from mailbox state. Ownership is a combinational function of the mailbox
registers, evaluated in the following precedence order.

```mermaid
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TD
    accTitle: MCU mailbox SRAM owner resolution
    accDescr: A decision tree resolving the single exclusive SRAM owner from the lock, release, zeroization, EXECUTE, TARGET_USER_VALID, and CMD_STATUS state.

    Q1{"MBOX_LOCK set?"}
    Q2{"Releasing or SRAM zeroizing?"}
    Q3{"EXECUTE = 1?"}
    Q4{"TARGET_USER_VALID = 1?"}
    Q5{"CMD_STATUS = BUSY?"}

    NONE(["No software owner"])
    TGTO(["TARGET_USER agent"])
    ROOTO(["Root AXI user"])
    HOLD(["Lock holder"])

    Q1 -- No --> NONE
    Q1 -- Yes --> Q2
    Q2 -- Yes --> NONE
    Q2 -- No --> Q3
    Q3 -- No --> HOLD
    Q3 -- Yes --> Q4
    Q4 -- No --> Q5
    Q4 -- Yes --> TGTO
    Q5 -- No --> HOLD
    Q5 -- Yes --> ROOTO
```

Because ownership is combinational, each register write below is what moves
the exclusive owner from one agent to the next.

| Event | New exclusive SRAM owner |
|---|---|
| MCI reset | Root, as the reset lock holder |
| `LOCK` read returns 0 | The reading agent becomes lock holder |
| `EXECUTE=1` while `TARGET_USER_VALID=0` | Root |
| Root writes `TARGET_USER_VALID=1` while `EXECUTE=1` | The agent named by `TARGET_USER` |
| Target writes terminal `TARGET_STATUS` | Root, and hardware clears `TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_USER_VALID` |
| MCU writes non-BUSY `CMD_STATUS` | Lock holder |
| SRAM owner writes `EXECUTE=0` | None, and hardware begins zeroization |
| Zeroization completes | None, `LOCK` clears and the mailbox is reusable |

Writing `EXECUTE=0` revokes all software SRAM access and enters zeroization.

`CMD`, `DLEN` and `EXECUTE` write access follows SRAM ownership. Only the
current SRAM owner may write them, and writes from any other agent are dropped.
The agent that produced the data in the SRAM is the agent that reports its
length. The Requester cannot change or abort a request once `EXECUTE=1` hands
it to Root, while Root or a Target can end the transaction with `EXECUTE=0`
while it owns the SRAM.

**NOTE**: Neither the Requester nor Root can reclaim the mailbox from a Target
that never writes a terminal `TARGET_STATUS` or `EXECUTE=0`. Only an MCI reset
recovers it.

relations.rationale: The test acquires the lock with EXECUTE=0, writes DLEN and SRAM data as lock holder, and checks the written data is present in SRAM. This shows the lock holder has SRAM write access in that state.
relations.missing: Ownership is never checked via the SRAM owner register. It does not check that other agents are denied, and it does not exercise the other branches of the decision tree.

relations.rationale: Caliptra acquires the lock with EXECUTE=0 and writes then reads back SRAM entries, so the lock holder's SRAM access in the locked, not-executing state is exercised.
relations.missing: The SRAM owner register is not checked, nor is denial of access to non-owners. Only the lock holder's write and read-back is verified.

relations.rationale: After warm reset the lock is retained and EXECUTE reads 0, and the SRAM owner is checked to be the Requester (reset lock holder).
relations.missing: Only the reset-state case is covered. The test does not acquire the lock through a LOCK read, nor check ownership with EXECUTE=0 during normal operation, nor check that other agents are excluded.

relations.rationale: The plan item intends to check that the MCU has full mailbox access while it holds the lock, which relates to lock-holder SRAM ownership.
relations.missing: The item is not specific about EXECUTE=0 or release/zeroization conditions. It does not describe checking the SRAM owner value or exclusion of other agents.

Specification section: docs/CaliptraSSIntegrationSpecification.md > MCI > Programming interface > MCU Mailbox (lines 2277-2290)


Each mailbox can be used for secure and restricted communication between external SoC entities, the MCU, and Caliptra core.  This communication channel is essential for exchanging control messages, status updates, and other critical information that the MCU will use to monitor system boot, firmware updates, and security critical operations. Mailboxes are designed to ensure that only authorized entities can access and communicate through it, preserving the integrity and security of the SoC operations.

The mailboxes are generic with some specific protocols and legal operations/accesses to ensure their secured and restricted aspect. The command, statuses, and data that are intepreted by the MCU microcontroller (uC), Caliptra uC or other SoC agent are not defined or enforced in this specification.

The MCU uC can function as an intermediary between agents such as Caliptra uC
and other SoC agents. MCU MBOX SRAM has one exclusive owner at a time, and MCU
accesses the SRAM only while it is that owner. See
[MCU Mailbox MCU Access](./CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md#mcu-mailbox-mcu-access)
for the MCU CSR access rules used by the flows below. Software can observe the
current owner through `MBOX_HW_STATUS.SRAM_OWNER`.

The [Caliptra SS HW MCU Mailbox Spec](./CaliptraSSHardwareSpecification.md#mcu-mailbox) has more details about the specific registers and interrupts used in the mailbox flows.

relations.rationale: Checks the HW_STATUS-reported SRAM owner matches the expected owner in each phase of the ownership flow, plus after the release race.
Reads SRAM_OWNER via the CSR and checks it is Root after execute and Target after the grant.
relations.missing: Does not check the owner in the other phases (Requester, release/return to Requester) or the initial owner.

relations.rationale: Reads sram_owner after warm reset and checks it is the Requester.
relations.missing: Only the post-warm-reset owner value is observed; owner changes across the flow are not checked.

relations.rationale: Checks per phase that only the expected owner reads/keeps SRAM data while all non-owners read 0 and writes are dropped, and HW_STATUS owner matches one expected owner.
Checks that before the target grant, non-owner target reads 0 and writes are dropped, and after the grant the target writes land in SRAM.
relations.missing: Does not check the SRAM owner field directly, and only covers MCU-to-Target handoff, not exclusivity across all owner phases.

relations.rationale: Non-owner agents including Root/MCU read 0 and have writes dropped in phases they do not own, while the owner reads its data.
MCU as Root writes SRAM only while it is the SRAM owner after execute, and checks the owner is Root. Also checks Root writes to CMD and EXECUTE have no effect once the Target owns the SRAM.
relations.missing: Does not check that MCU SRAM reads/writes are blocked while it is not the owner.

relations.rationale: Plan item states valid users lacking permission, e.g. without lock, get writes dropped and reads of 0 on SRAM; generic to any requester.
relations.missing: Not specific to MCU as non-owner, and no check of MCU access tied to SRAM ownership.
